extracted.intended_audience: manufacturers, industrial managers, business owners, and those organizing production and finance
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for organizing manufacturing, pricing, purchasing, labor, and plant layout so as to maximize service to consumers, reduce costs, and stabilize business through efficiency and standardization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Business exists to serve the consumer
rubrics_metrics.description: The only reason for growing crops, for mining, or for manufacturing, is that people may eat, keep warm, have clothing to wear, and articles to use. The manufacturer is an instrument of society and can serve society only as he manages his enterprises so as to turn over to the public an increasingly better product at an ever-decreasing price, and at the same time to pay to all those who have a hand in his business an ever-increasing wage, based upon the work they do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge prosperity by comfort of the people, not the manufacturer's bank balance; serve consumers by quality or price, ideally highest quality at lowest price. Business should be reorganized on the basis of service rather than speculation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set price to meet buying power (price-first strategy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prices are based on an estimate of what the largest possible number of people will want to pay, or can pay, for what we have to sell. Reduction of price comes first; then the firm forces costs down to meet that price.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Name a low price to force everyone to seek efficiencies and innovation; this often yields more discoveries about manufacturing than leisurely cost studies. The usual cost-first method may be 'scientific' narrowly but not in the broad sense if it produces an unaffordable product.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid cutting wages as a first response
rubrics_metrics.description: Cutting wages is the easiest and most slovenly way to handle business downturns and is inhuman; it shifts managerial incompetence onto labor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tackle management and efficiency issues before reducing wages. Paying high wages can increase worker efficiency and reduce overall costs; use wages as an incentive based on work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep production and business activity going (avoid idleness)
rubrics_metrics.description: A man in business can either take a direct loss and continue to do business or stop doing business and take the loss of idleness, which is often greater and saps initiative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer taking part of past profits (write-downs) to keep business moving; prolonged shutdowns destroy energy to restart; keep factories running where practical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Buy only for immediate production requirements (no speculation)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not worth while to buy for other than immediate needs. Buying ahead for speculative purposes enters into a guessing contest and does not pay over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid bargain lots in excess of requirements; buy the best price for the quantity required; recognize transportation constraints; speculative buying-ahead gains are typically offset by later losses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjust prices decisively to clear inventory
rubrics_metrics.description: When stock will not move, reduce the price decisively (take a 'big bite') rather than nibbling at it; get the stuff out rather than encourage customers to wait for further cuts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Taking losses on inventory can be wise to keep community commerce moving; nibbling at price prolongs problems and harms demand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standardization and interchangeability (long-lasting products)
rubrics_metrics.description: Standardization is the final stage of the process: start with the consumer, work back through design, and finally arrive at manufacturing. Parts of a specific model are interchangeable with all other cars of that model and with similar parts on all cars turned out previously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not practice planned obsolescence; aim to make machines that will 'last forever' and allow customers to update old models with current parts cheaply, thus serving the consumer and reducing waste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use service as guiding industrial idea, not speculation for profit
rubrics_metrics.description: The true industrial idea is to express a serviceable idea, to duplicate a useful idea, by as many thousands as there are people who need it. The negation is making a profit out of speculation instead of work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Business should be cooperation among many forces and interests; avoid strategies aiming to maximize immediate extraction from consumers (e.g., selling obsolete replacements).

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuous experiment and scrap/utilization economy
rubrics_metrics.description: Constant experiments in utilization of scrap and waste lead to savings (examples: using stamped-out discs for radiator caps, upsetting-machine bolts using less material). Sweepings and scrap can amount to significant annual savings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage workers to find uses for waste; small savings ('a penny here and a penny there') compound to large annual amounts; reinvest in process improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vertical integration and by-product utilization
rubrics_metrics.description: Integrate back to raw sources and processes where feasible (own mines, railways, coke ovens, blast furnaces) to control quality and reduce costs; use by-products (gas, ammonium sulphate, benzol) to fuel plants or sell.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invest in facilities that turn otherwise wasted by-products into fuel, fertilizer, or revenue; pipe gases internally and use mechanical handling to eliminate manual steps and extra meltings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Locate production where parts can be made most economically
rubrics_metrics.description: Assemble near markets and have branches produce parts when they can do so more cheaply than the central plant; decentralize assembly to reduce transportation and packing costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: ship parts to assembling stations rather than completed cars; put shops where water power or local advantages exist; build farmer-industrialist arrangements when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply machinery to increase human productivity and role of service
rubrics_metrics.description: For most purposes a man with a machine is better than a man without a machine; design products and manufacturing to multiply the power of the hand so the worker has a larger service role and is entitled to a larger share of comfort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use machinery design to raise the worker's contribution and justify higher wages; mechanization reduces time per unit of human input.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid elaborate, costly administration and monuments
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not erect elaborate buildings as monuments to success; the interest and upkeep add uselessly to product cost and may indicate excessive administration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer to be advertised by product, not by where the product is made; keep administrative overhead lean to avoid increasing prices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use price reductions to pressure efficiency and discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: Naming a price low enough forces everybody in the place to the highest point of efficiency; the low price 'makes everybody dig for profits.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat price reduction as a tool to catalyze process innovation and organization improvements rather than just a margin squeeze.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study competitors' products to learn and improve
rubrics_metrics.description: Buy one of every new car that comes out, put it through a road test, take it apart, and study how and of what everything is made in order to discover features that might be developed and adapted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reverse-engineering competitor offerings and learning from them is an explicit policy; doing so publicly can attract comment but is a continuous innovation source.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat economic fluctuations as management challenges
rubrics_metrics.description: Each depression should be regarded as a challenge to the brains of the business community to increase management quality and overcome difficulties without resorting to wage cuts or speculation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Management should aim to reorganize business and finance gradually toward service-based systems; individual firms can begin improvements which will have broader influence over time.
